content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies the winograd transformation for 3D convolutional neural network. As the winograd parameters are large in 3D filters, low-rank trainable parameters are introduced in the winograd domain to reduce the training FLOPs. A low-rank oriented sparse granularity is further introduced to regularly prune the winograd weights and achieve speedups in the test phase. Experiments conducts on 3D CNNs demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

+ This paper studies an important problem of 3D neural network acclerating since the 3D network have much more parameters and FLOPs than those of 2D CNNs. 

+ The proposed method can reduce both the training and testing paramters and costs, which is energy saving.

+ This paper is well written and easy to understand.

Weaknesses:

- The novelty of the proposed method is limited. The proposed method consists of three parts: 3D winograd, low-rank transformation and regular sparse. Although it is new to apply low-rank transformation in 3D winograd transformation, the idea itself is off-the-shelf with few adaptation in the 3D nerual network. For the Sparse Granularity part, this proposed method is adapted from Taylor pruning. 

- Important litertures are missing. There are many works [1,2,3,4,5] in pruning 3D networks and 3D winograd transformation, while this paper fails to make a comparison and discussion with them. Therefore, the superiority of the proposed method compared with existing works is unknown.

- Lack of ablation studies. As the proposed method consists of 3D winograd, low-rank transformation and regular sparse. It is essential to study the effectiveness of each component. Several important ablations are missing, such as: 1) only applying 3D winograd transformation; 2) the training FLOPs saving using low-rank transformation; 3) regular pruning without low-rank transformation. 

[1] Pruning 3D Filters For Accelerating 3D ConvNets. IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON MULTIMEDIA 2020,

[2] Three-dimensional convolutional neural network pruning with regularizationbased method. ICIP 2019.

[3] Frequency Domain Compact 3D Convolutional Neural Networks. CVPR 2020.

[4] 3D Winograd Layer with Regular Mask Pruning. ICMEW 2022.

[5] Winograd Algorithm for 3D Convolution Neural Networks. ICANN 2017.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The overall writing of this paper is clear and easy to follow. The novelty of the proposed method is limited and many important litertures are missing.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, the paper needs to add more comparison and discussion with related works. It is also lacking in novelty as mentioned above.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents a low-rank Winograd transformation, which eliminates the redundant parameters and drives the updating towards main directions of the whole Winograd space. In addition, the authors also introduce a low-rank oriented sparse granularity to purchase effectual speedups.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
This paper presents a low-rank Winograd transformation to reduce the over- parameterized issue in 3D CNNs.

Weakness:
1/ The motivation of this paper is unreasonable. In this paper, the low-rankness of the Winograd-domain weight matrix is demonstrated in Fig. 2. Building upon this, the authors infer that the residual of the pre-trained Winograd-domain weight matrix is also low-rank. In my opinion, this inference is not rigorous. There is no direct relevance between the low-rankness of the Winograd-domain weight matrix and the pre-trained Winograd-domain weight matrix residual, it depends on the nature of the pre-trained Winograd-domain weight matrix.

2/ There are too few competing methods in the part of experiments. Readers cannot tell whether this approach achieves SOTA performance.

3/ The section of literature review is inadequate. There is no mention of methods that focus on the Winograd transform of 3D CNNs. Such methods should be described to help the reader better evaluate the proposed methods

4/ Many claims in this paper are not easy to follow. For example, the authors claim that [1-3] derive irregular sparse weight matrix, but the proposed method leads to regular sparse weight matrix. What is the basis of this claim?  Relevant theoretical analysis is necessary

5/ The experiments are insufficient. In this paper, a speedup mechanism is proposed. But there are no experiments about the inference time. 

6/ The purpose of Sec. 4.2.1 is to validate the effectiveness of low-rank Winograd transformation, i.e., the reduction of the trainable parameters. But there is  no parameter scale analysis in this section. 

7/ In Sec. 4.2.2, there is no need to show the results on model R3D-18, and R3D-34. Because such experiments cannot demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method.


[1] Song Han, Jeff Pool, John Tran, and William Dally. Learning both weights and connections for efficient neural network. 28, 2015b. 
[2] Yann LeCun, John Denker, and Sara Solla. Optimal brain damage. In Proceedings of the Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS), 1989. 
[3] Jonathan Frankle and Michael Carbin. The lottery ticket hypothesis: Finding sparse, trainable neural networks. In International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR), 2018.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
1/ The clarity of this paper is not very good. Many claims are not easy to understand. 
2/ The quality of this paper is below the borderline of the conference.
3/ The novelty of this paper fails to meet the requirements of the conference.
4/ This paper is easy to reproduce, since all of the detailed experiment settings are provided.

Weakness

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a low-rank/pruning algorithm for accelerating the training of 3D CNN network when using Winograd convolutions. It explains some difficulties of extending the commonly used Winograd algorithms from 2D to 3D, which results in an increased of intermediate parameters, and reverts to training the intermediate parameters instead. Therefore the method can make use of different pruning options.  The method is compared on replicating standard 3D convolution performance on two video datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths**
- In general the concept of speeding up 3D convolutions can have great practical impact
- The paper goes in much detail on the required elementwise products to obtain the desired output and how those can be approximated with lower ranks
- The results are evaluated on a mobile computing device
- Different trade-off ratios are considered

**Weaknesses**
- The paper is at times hard to follow and I would have preferred a better motivation
- There are competing uncited works (e.g. https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/978-3-319-68612-7_69.pdf) that use 3D Winograd as a drop-in (black-box) algorithm to train 3D CNNs in a normal way and also achieve good speed-ups compared to CuDNN without loss of accuracy, I think this should be discussed and put in context
- Orthogonal to that comment: there are many competing works for pruning network parameters through either low-rank approximations (cf. 10.1109/TPAMI.2015.2502579), quantisation (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.media.2021.102200) or network slimming (this was already mentioned in manuscript), but those are not really considered as comparison
- The application does not include (medical) 3D volumetric images, which would be of obvious practical use for accelerated 3D CNNs
- In terms of real-world speed-up the presentation of FLOPs itself may be misleading, because nearly all current GPUs support specific hardware speed-ups for tensor operations (ie matrix multiplications) that might be unusable with the proposed method. The statement "the model is able to improve the speed of winograd domain operations .." is unclear (does this take into account that repeated re-training might be necessary?), it would be important to see overall speed-up for the whole training in comparison to a CuDNN (or related) optimised pipeline for a given CNN.
- Minor: there are often typos e.g. "bset accuracy" and the fonts in figures are often too small. The tables could also be more focussed
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: I value the ideas for low-rank approximations and attempts to speed up 3D convolutions, a topic that seems to be understudied. There is some technical novelty, but the practical impact is limited in my opinion (see comments about practical speed-ups). Overall the current submission feels unfocused and not ready for publication, as it mixes many ideas without thorough analysis and comparisons to related work (see above for details). The paper itself gives sufficient details for reproducibility, however the immense complexity makes re-implementation unlikely. I would therefore recommend to release source code.
content.summary_of_the_review: I currently cannot recommend acceptance, because the detailed technical contributions do not translate into enough significance for a larger audience at the current stage.

content.title: Low-Rank Winograd Transformation for 3D Convolutional Neural Networks
content.abstract: This paper focuses on Winograd transformation in 3D convolutional neural networks (CNNs) that are more over-parameterized compared with the common 2-D version. The over-increasing Winograd parameters not only exacerbate training complexity but also barricade the practical speedups due simply to the volume of element-wise products in the Winograd domain. We attempt to reduce trainable parameters by introducing a low-rank Winograd transformation, a novel training paradigm that decouples the original large tensor into two less storage-required trainable tensors, leading to a significant complexity reduction. Built upon our low-rank Winograd transformation, we take one step ahead by proposing a low-rank oriented sparse granularity that measures column-wise parameter importance. By simply involving the non-zero columns in the element-wise product, our sparse granularity is empowered with the ability to produce a very regular sparse pattern to acquire effectual Winograd speedups. To better understand the efficacy of our method, we perform extensive experiments upon 3D CNNs. Results manifest that our low-rank Winograd transformation well outperforms the vanilla Winograd transformation. We also show that our proposed low-rank oriented sparse granularity permits practical Winograd acceleration compared with the vanilla counterpart.
